ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₃er-der. Proto-Germanic *arwaz Proto-Germanic *garwaz Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Germanic *-janą Proto-Germanic *garwijanąder. Old Norse gervibor. Middle English gere English gear From Middle English gere, a borrowing from Old Norse gervi, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną (“to prepare”). See also adjective yare, yar from the same root via Old English.

senses.d: Equipment or paraphernalia, especially that used for an athletic endeavor.

ex: Aray thy selfe in her most gorgeous geare
Those Eastern winters, ⁠I can't endure 'em / So every year I pack my gear and come out here till Purim / Rosh Hashanah, I spend in Arizona

senses.d: A wheel, wheel segment, or bar with grooves (teeth) engraved on the outer circumference, such that two such devices can interlock and convey motion from one to the other.
ex: Near-synonyms: (wheel types) cog, cogwheel, gear wheel, gearwheel

senses.d: A particular combination or choice of interlocking gears, such that a particular gear ratio is achieved; often selected via a shifter.
A configuration of the transmission of a motor car so as to achieve a particular ratio of engine to axle torque.

ex: goe they both together to their geare.

senses.d: To provide with gearing; to fit with gears in order to achieve a desired gear ratio.
To be in gear, come into gear.
To dress; to put gear on; to harness.
To design or devise (something) so as to be suitable (for a particular type of person or a particular purpose).
ex: This shop is not really geared towards people of our age.
They have geared the hotel mainly at tourists.

senses.d: To borrow money in order to invest it in assets.
